recipes.name: Sandwich bread
recipes.summary: A soft white loaf for toast and sandwiches, sized for the loaf pan you have.

ingredients.prep: or bread flour; spoon it into the cup and level it

steps: Warm the milk and water to about 110°F: warm on your wrist, not hot. Stir in the sugar and yeast and let it stand 5 to 10 minutes, until foamy.
Add the butter, salt and about two-thirds of the flour and stir until smooth. Work in the rest of the flour a little at a time until the dough pulls away from the bowl.

Knead on a lightly floured counter 8 to 10 minutes (5 to 6 in a stand mixer with a dough hook), until smooth and springy. If it sticks, add flour a spoonful at a time; a slightly tacky dough makes a softer loaf.
Put the dough in a greased bowl, cover, and let it rise in a warm spot until doubled, 1 to 1½ hours.
Grease the pan. Press the dough into a rectangle as wide as the pan is long, roll it up tightly from the short side, pinch the seam, and set it seam side down in the pan.
Cover and let it rise until the top crowns about 1 inch over the rim of the pan, 45 to 60 minutes. Heat the oven to 350°F for the last 20 minutes.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes for a 9 × 5 pan (30 to 35 for 8½ × 4½), until deep golden and the center reads about 190°F. If the top browns fast, lay foil over it after 20 minutes.
Turn the loaf out onto a rack and cool at least 1 hour before slicing; it is still setting inside.
No loaf pan? Shape the dough into a 10-inch oval on a greased or parchment-lined baking sheet, let it rise 45 minutes, and bake 30 to 35 minutes.

stages.do: Shape the loaves and set them in the pans
Cool on a rack before slicing

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, about 3 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: Yeast and salt go by the flour’s weight: 7 g yeast (a packet) and 9 g salt for every 480 g of flour. For two loaves, double everything and bake the pans side by side with space between them; rising and baking take the same time, not twice as long. Most stand mixers knead dough for two 9 × 5 loaves at most. For less than a full packet, weigh the yeast; a ¾ batch for an 8½ × 4½ pan takes about 5 g.
recipes.old_way: The first factory-made yeast in the United States went on sale in the late 1860s (the Fleischmann brothers in Cincinnati, 1868). Before that, home bakers raised their bread with a starter kept from batch to batch or with yeast from brewing.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Bread flour gives a taller, chewier loaf; all-purpose gives a softer one. Both work.
recipes.yield: One 9 × 5-inch loaf (about 1¾ lb), 16 slices about ½ inch thick. The same dough at ¾ size fills an 8½ × 4½-inch pan (12 slices).

recipes.name: Whole-wheat sandwich bread
recipes.summary: All whole-wheat flour, a little honey, and a rest before kneading so the bran softens.
steps: Warm the milk and water to about 110°F. Stir in the honey and yeast and let it stand 5 to 10 minutes, until foamy.
Stir in the flour, butter and salt to make a sticky, shaggy dough. Cover and let it rest 20 minutes: whole-wheat flour soaks up water slowly, and the dough gets easier to knead.
Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and stretchy but still a little tacky. Add flour only a spoonful at a time; too much makes a dry, heavy loaf.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, 1 to 1½ hours.
Shape it like sandwich bread (press into a rectangle, roll up tightly, pinch the seam) and set it in a greased pan.
Let it rise until it crowns about 1 inch over the rim, 45 to 60 minutes, while the oven heats to 350°F.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes (8½ × 4½: 30 to 35), until the center reads about 190°F. Cool on a rack at least 1 hour before slicing.

stages.do: Mix, rest and knead the dough
Shape the loaves and set them in the pans
Cool on a rack before slicing

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, about 3 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: 7 g yeast and 9 g salt for every 480 g of flour. Whole wheat rises a little slower in a cool kitchen; go by the size of the dough, not the clock.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Half whole-wheat and half white flour gives a lighter loaf: see the half whole-wheat recipe.
recipes.yield: One 9 × 5-inch loaf, 16 slices about ½ inch thick (¾ of the dough fills an 8½ × 4½-inch pan).

recipes.name: Half whole-wheat sandwich bread
recipes.summary: Half whole-wheat, half white flour, sweetened with a little honey: a soft loaf for sandwiches.
steps: Warm the milk and water to about 110°F. Stir in the honey and yeast and let it stand 5 to 10 minutes, until foamy.
Stir in the whole-wheat flour, butter and salt, then add the white flour a little at a time until the dough comes together. Let it rest 10 minutes so the bran softens.
Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Whole-wheat dough stays a little tacky; add flour sparingly.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, 1 to 1½ hours (whole wheat can be a little slower).
Shape it as for sandwich bread: press into a rectangle, roll up tightly, pinch the seam, and set it in a greased pan.
Let it rise until it crowns about 1 inch over the rim, 45 to 60 minutes, while the oven heats to 350°F.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes (8½ × 4½: 30 to 35), until the center reads about 190°F. Cool on a rack at least 1 hour before slicing.

stages.do: Mix, rest and knead the dough
Shape the loaves and set them in the pans
Cool on a rack before slicing

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, about 3 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: Same rules as sandwich bread: 7 g yeast and 9 g salt for every 480 g of flour in all. Double for two loaves; the times stay the same.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: For an all whole-wheat loaf, see whole-wheat sandwich bread.
recipes.yield: One 9 × 5-inch loaf, 16 slices about ½ inch thick (¾ of the dough fills an 8½ × 4½-inch pan).

recipes.name: French bread and baguettes
recipes.summary: Flour, water, yeast and salt, baked hot for a crackly crust: two French loaves or three thin baguettes.
steps: Stir the yeast into the warm water and let it stand 5 minutes. Add the flour and salt and mix to a shaggy dough.
Knead about 10 minutes, until smooth and stretchy. The dough should be soft and a little sticky.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, 1½ to 2 hours.
Divide in two. Pat each piece into a rectangle and roll it up tightly into a 12- to 14-inch log, pinching the seam. Set them seam down on a floured or parchment-lined baking sheet, well apart.
Baguettes instead: divide into 3, roll each up into a log, rest 10 minutes, then roll it under your palms from the middle out to a thin 15-inch rope. Bake them 20 to 25 minutes in the next steps.
Cover loosely and let them rise until puffy, 45 to 60 minutes. Put an empty metal pan on the lowest rack and heat the oven to 450°F.
Slash the tops 3 or 4 times with a sharp knife. Slide the loaves in and pour 1 cup of hot water into the metal pan for steam (stand back).
Bake 25 to 30 minutes, until deep brown and hollow-sounding when tapped underneath (about 200°F inside). Cool on a rack at least 30 minutes.

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, then crisp it in a 350°F oven for 5 to 10 minutes.

keeps: Counter: best the day it’s baked; keep it in a paper bag up to about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread), crisping it in a hot oven before serving.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: 12 g salt and 7 g yeast per 600 g flour. A half batch makes one loaf (weigh 3.5 g yeast). Two batches bake fine on two sheets if you switch their places halfway.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
Pour the steam water carefully and keep your face back from the oven door.
recipes.yield: Two loaves, about 1 lb each, or three 15-inch baguettes.

recipes.name: Pizza dough
recipes.summary: A one-pound ball of dough, the size sold at the store, ready in about 1½ hours.
steps: Stir the yeast into the warm water and let it stand 5 minutes.
Add the flour, salt and olive oil and mix to a rough dough. Knead 6 to 8 minutes until smooth.
Put it in an oiled bowl, cover, and let it rise until doubled, 1 to 1½ hours. It is now ready to stretch and top.
If the dough springs back as you stretch it, cover it and let it rest 10 minutes, then try again.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator overnight, then let it sit on the counter, covered, about 1 hour before stretching.

keeps: Refrigerator: in an oiled, covered container until the next day; it keeps rising slowly, so punch it down.
Freezer: wrap the risen ball airtight, up to about 1 month; longer, and the yeast weakens (NDSU and University of Missouri give about a month for unbaked yeast dough).
recipes.scaling: Each 1-lb ball takes 280 g flour, 4 g yeast and 6 g salt. A packet (7 g) of yeast is close enough for two balls.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
recipes.yield: One 1-lb ball of dough: one 14-inch round pizza or one 10 × 15-inch sheet pan.

recipes.name: Oatmeal bread
recipes.summary: Rolled oats soaked in hot water with honey and butter make a soft, faintly sweet, moist loaf.
steps: Pour the boiling water over the oats, honey, butter and salt in a large bowl. Let it stand until just warm, about 110°F, 20 to 30 minutes.
Warm the milk to about 110°F, stir in the yeast, and let it stand 5 minutes. Add it to the oats.
Stir in the flour a cup at a time. Knead 8 minutes until smooth; the oats keep it a little sticky.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 to 1½ hours.
Shape into a loaf, set it in a greased pan, and let it rise until it crowns 1 inch over the rim, 45 to 60 minutes. Heat the oven to 350°F.
Sprinkle a few oats on top if you like. Bake 35 to 40 minutes, until the center reads about 190°F. Cool at least 1 hour.

stages.do: Shape and set in the pan

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, about 3 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: Scales by the loaf; keep 7 g yeast and 9 g salt per batch.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Potato bread
recipes.summary: Mashed potato and its cooking water make a tender, moist loaf that stays soft for days.
steps: Boil the potato in water until very tender, about 15 minutes. Save ½ cup of the cooking water, drain, and mash the potato smooth (about ¾ cup).
Stir the butter and sugar into the warm potato, then the milk and saved potato water. Let it cool to about 110°F and stir in the yeast.
Beat in the egg and salt, then the flour a little at a time. Knead 8 minutes; the dough is soft and slightly sticky.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 hour (potato dough is quick).
Shape into a loaf, set it in a greased pan, and let it rise until it crowns about 1 inch over the rim, 40 to 50 minutes. Heat the oven to 375°F.
Bake 30 to 35 minutes, until golden and about 190°F in the center. Cool at least 1 hour.

stages.do: Cool, mix and knead the dough
Shape and set in the pan

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, about 3 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: One medium russet (about ¾ cup mashed) per loaf. Leftover plain mashed potato works; skip the boiling.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: A good use for garden potatoes.

recipes.name: Deli-style rye bread
recipes.summary: A light rye with caraway seeds, the kind for corned beef or turkey sandwiches.
steps: Stir the yeast and molasses into the warm water and let it stand 5 minutes.
Add the oil, salt, caraway, rye flour and bread flour and mix to a soft dough. Rye dough is stickier than wheat dough; wet your hands instead of adding much flour.
Knead about 6 minutes until fairly smooth. Cover and let it rise until about doubled, 1 to 1½ hours.
Shape into an oval loaf on a baking sheet dusted with cornmeal or flour (or into a greased loaf pan). Cover and let it rise until puffy, 45 to 60 minutes. Heat the oven to 375°F.
Brush the top with water and slash it 3 times. Bake 35 to 40 minutes, until it sounds hollow underneath and reads about 190°F.
Cool completely, 2 hours, before slicing; rye stays gummy while warm.

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, about 3 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: Keep rye at about a third of the flour; more rye makes a denser loaf that needs a different method.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
Rye has gluten, and this bread is mostly wheat flour: it isn’t gluten-free.
recipes.yield: One oval loaf (or a 9 × 5-inch pan loaf), about 16 slices.

recipes.name: Italian bread
recipes.summary: A soft-crusted, golden loaf with a little olive oil and sugar, often topped with sesame seeds.
steps: Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm water and let it stand 5 minutes. Add the oil, salt and flour and mix.
Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 to 1½ hours.
Shape into a 14-inch log (or two 10-inch logs), set on a baking sheet dusted with cornmeal, and let it rise until puffy, 45 to 60 minutes. Heat the oven to 425°F.
Brush with water, sprinkle with sesame seeds if you like, and slash one long cut down the top.
Bake 25 to 30 minutes, until golden and hollow-sounding (about 200°F). Cool 30 minutes.

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping, then warm in a 350°F oven for 5 to 10 minutes.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: 10 g salt and 7 g yeast per 500 g flour.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
recipes.yield: One large loaf, about 1¾ lb (or two smaller ones).

recipes.name: Focaccia
recipes.summary: A wet, olive-oil dough baked in a sheet pan: crisp underneath, airy inside, dimpled on top.
steps: Stir the flour, yeast and salt in a bowl, add the water, and mix until no dry flour is left. The dough will be very wet; that’s right.
Cover and rest 30 minutes. With a wet hand, lift one side of the dough and fold it over the middle; turn the bowl and repeat 4 times. Do this 3 times, 30 minutes apart.
Pour ¼ cup of the oil into the pan, tip the dough in, and turn it once to coat. Let it rest 20 minutes, then gently stretch it toward the corners.
Cover and let it rise until puffy and bubbly, 45 to 60 minutes. Heat the oven to 450°F.
Drizzle with the rest of the oil, press deep dimples all over with oiled fingers, and sprinkle with rosemary and coarse salt.
Bake 20 to 25 minutes, until deep golden on top and underneath. Cool 10 minutes in the pan, then move it to a rack.

stages.do: Pan it and let it rise

plan.thaw: Thaw, then warm in a 375°F oven 5 to 8 minutes.

keeps: Counter: best the day it’s baked; wrapped, about 2 days, recrisped in the oven.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: Double it in a half-sheet pan (13 × 18 inch); the baking time stays about the same.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: The wet dough is what makes the big holes; resist adding flour.

recipes.name: Ciabatta
recipes.summary: Very wet dough, folded instead of kneaded, baked into two flat, open-holed loaves.
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, salt, water and oil until no dry flour remains. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
With a wet hand, stretch and fold the dough over itself 4 times, turning the bowl. Repeat 3 more times, every 30 minutes. Then let it rise undisturbed until doubled and bubbly, about 1 more hour.
Tip it onto a well-floured counter. With floured hands, gently pat it into a rectangle and cut it in two. Fold each piece in thirds like a letter and set them seam side down on floured parchment.
Cover and let them rise 45 minutes while the oven heats to 450°F with a baking sheet inside.
Flip each loaf over onto the hot sheet (parchment and all) so the floured side is up. Bake 22 to 25 minutes, until deep golden. Cool at least 30 minutes.

stages.do: Stretch and fold 4 times, then rise

plan.thaw: Thaw, then crisp in a 350°F oven 5 to 10 minutes.

keeps: Counter: best the day it’s baked; in a paper bag, about 2 days.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: Don’t add flour to make it easier to handle; flour your hands and the counter instead.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
recipes.yield: Two loaves, about 14 oz each, or 8 sandwich rolls.

recipes.name: Sub rolls
recipes.summary: Long, soft-crusted rolls for subs, hoagies and meatball sandwiches.
steps: Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm water and let it stand 5 minutes. Add the oil, salt and flour and mix.
Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth. Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
Divide into 8 pieces (about 100 g each). Pat each into a rectangle, roll it up tightly into an 8-inch log, and set them 2 inches apart on the sheets.
Cover and let rise until puffy, 40 to 50 minutes. Heat the oven to 400°F.
Brush with water and slash each down the middle if you like. Bake 18 to 20 minutes, until golden. Cool on a rack.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter, about 1 hour.

keeps: Counter: in a bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls).
Freezer: bag them once cool, up to 3 months (University of Missouri).
recipes.scaling: Each roll is an eighth of the dough; the planner counts rolls.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Soft breadsticks
recipes.summary: Pizza-style dough cut into sticks and brushed with garlic butter and Parmesan.
steps: Make the dough: stir the yeast into the warm water, add the flour, salt and oil, and knead 6 to 8 minutes. Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
Pat it into a 12 × 8-inch rectangle on a greased baking sheet and cut it into 12 strips with a pizza cutter (leave them side by side). Let rise 20 minutes. Heat the oven to 400°F.
Brush with half the garlic butter and sprinkle with Parmesan. Bake 15 to 18 minutes, until golden. Brush with the rest of the butter and pull apart.

plan.thaw: Warm frozen breadsticks in a 350°F oven about 10 minutes.

keeps: Counter: in a bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls).
Freezer: bag them once cool, up to 3 months (University of Missouri).
recipes.scaling: Same dough as one 1-lb ball of pizza dough.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: English muffins
recipes.summary: A soft, wet dough cut into rounds, rolled in cornmeal and cooked slowly on a griddle.
steps: Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm milk and water and let it stand 5 minutes. Add the butter, salt and flour and beat to a soft, sticky dough.
Knead about 5 minutes (in a mixer is easiest). Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
Pat it ¾ inch thick on a floured counter and cut 3-inch rounds. Press the scraps together once for the last few.
Set the rounds on a sheet dusted with cornmeal, dust the tops, cover, and let them rise 30 to 45 minutes.

Heat a dry griddle over medium-low. Cook the muffins a few at a time, 7 to 8 minutes per side, until browned and the sides spring back (about 200°F in the middle). Keep the heat low so the inside cooks before the outside burns.
Cool on a rack. Split them with a fork for the craggy, crisp-toasting inside.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter, about 1 hour.

keeps: Counter: in a bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls).
Freezer: bag them once cool, up to 3 months (University of Missouri).
recipes.scaling: Each muffin is a tenth of the dough. Cook in batches; a griddle holds 4 to 6.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Soft buns and dinner rolls
recipes.summary: One soft dough for hamburger buns, hot dog buns or a pan of dinner rolls.
equipment: 2 baking sheets (or a 9 × 13 pan for rolls)
steps: Warm the milk and water to about 110°F. Stir in the sugar and yeast and let it stand 5 to 10 minutes, until foamy.
Beat in the egg, butter and salt, then add the flour a little at a time to make a soft dough.
Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and springy. Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 to 1½ hours.
Divide the dough. A kitchen scale makes even buns: for a full batch, about 95 g per hamburger or hot dog bun, or 60 g per dinner roll.

Hamburger buns: round each piece into a tight ball, set it on a greased sheet, and flatten to about 3½ inches. Hot dog buns: roll each piece into a 6-inch log and set them 2 inches apart. Dinner rolls: round into balls and set them almost touching in a greased 9 × 13 pan.
Cover and let rise until puffy, 40 to 50 minutes. Heat the oven to 375°F.
Bake until golden brown, 15 to 18 minutes for buns and 15 to 20 for rolls (about 190°F in the center). Brush the tops with melted butter if you like, and cool on a rack.

stages.do: Divide and shape the buns or rolls

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter, about 1 hour.

keeps: Counter: in a bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls).
Freezer: bag them once cool, up to 3 months (University of Missouri).
recipes.scaling: The planner adds up buns and rolls together: each hamburger or hot dog bun takes a tenth of a batch and each dinner roll a sixteenth. Yeast and salt follow the flour by weight (7 g yeast and 9 g salt per 500 g flour). Round the egg to a whole one; for a half batch, beat one egg and use half.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Homemade buns are bigger and heavier than store buns, so nutrition per bun is higher.
recipes.yield: 10 hamburger buns (about 3½ inches across), 10 hot dog buns, or 16 dinner rolls, or a mix of shapes from one batch.

recipes.name: Japanese-style milk bread
recipes.summary: A cooked flour-and-milk paste (tangzhong) makes an extra-soft, fluffy loaf that stays fresh longer.

ingredients.prep: 20 g of it for the paste
100 g of it for the paste

steps: Paste: whisk 20 g (2 tablespoons plus 1 teaspoon) of the flour into 100 g (scant ½ cup) of the milk in a small pan. Cook over medium-low, whisking, until it thickens like pudding and the whisk leaves lines, 2 to 3 minutes. Cool to lukewarm.
Warm the rest of the milk to about 110°F and stir in the yeast. Add the paste, egg, sugar, salt and the rest of the flour and mix.
Knead 10 minutes (it starts sticky), then knead in the butter a little at a time and knead 5 to 10 minutes more, until very smooth and stretchy.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
Divide into 3 pieces. Roll each into an oval, fold in the long sides, and roll it up from the short end. Set the 3 rolls side by side in the greased pan.
Let rise until the top is about ½ inch over the rim, 45 to 60 minutes. Heat the oven to 350°F. Brush with milk.
Bake 30 to 35 minutes, until deep golden and about 190°F in the middle. Cool in the pan 10 minutes, then on a rack.

stages.do: Cook the paste and cool it
Mix and knead in the butter

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, about 3 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: The paste is about 6% of the flour cooked with five times its weight in milk; scale both with the loaf.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Iowa State Extension notes the cooked-paste method makes bread softer and helps it keep longer.

recipes.name: Challah
recipes.summary: A braided egg bread sweetened with honey, shiny with egg wash.
steps: Stir the yeast and a spoonful of the honey into the warm water and let it stand 5 minutes.
Beat in the rest of the honey, the oil, 2 eggs and the salt, then the flour. Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, 1½ to 2 hours.
Divide into 3 (or 6) equal pieces and roll each into a 16-inch rope. Pinch the ends together and braid loosely, then pinch and tuck the other end under.
Set on the sheet, brush with beaten egg, and let rise until puffy, about 1 hour. Heat the oven to 350°F. Brush again.
Bake 30 to 35 minutes, until deep brown and about 190°F in the thickest part. Cool on a rack.

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, about 3 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls). Cornell Extension advises against keeping bread in the refrigerator.

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: Two loaves: double it and braid two. A day-old loaf makes excellent French toast.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Made with oil, so it has no dairy.
recipes.yield: One large braided loaf, about 1¾ lb.

recipes.name: Brioche (loaf or buns)
recipes.summary: Eggs and lots of butter make a rich, tender bread; the dough rests overnight in the refrigerator.
equipment: stand mixer with dough hook (strongly recommended)
steps: Mix the flour, yeast, salt and sugar in the mixer bowl. Add the milk and 4 eggs and knead on medium-low about 5 minutes, until smooth.
With the mixer running, add the butter a piece at a time, waiting until each disappears. Knead 8 to 10 minutes more, until the dough is glossy and pulls from the sides.
Cover and let it rise 1 hour at room temperature, then press it down, cover tightly, and refrigerate overnight (8 to 16 hours). Cold dough is much easier to shape.
Shape while cold: a loaf (8 small balls in two rows in a greased 9 × 5 pan) or 8 buns flattened to 3½ inches on a lined sheet.
Let rise in a warm spot until puffy, 1½ to 2 hours. Heat the oven to 375°F for buns or 350°F for a loaf. Brush with beaten egg.
Bake buns 15 to 18 minutes; a loaf 35 to 40 minutes (cover with foil if it browns too fast). It’s done at about 190°F. Cool on a rack.

stages.do: Mix and knead in the butter

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter.

keeps: Counter: in a bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls).
Freezer: bag them once cool, up to 3 months (University of Missouri).
recipes.scaling: Keep the butter about 45% of the flour’s weight. A stand mixer handles up to a double batch.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Brioche buns are a favorite for burgers.

recipes.name: Cinnamon rolls
recipes.summary: A soft milk dough rolled around butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, finished with a simple glaze.

ingredients.prep: softened: half for the dough, half for the filling

equipment: unflavored dental floss or a sharp knife
steps: Stir the yeast into the warm milk. Add the sugar, egg, half the butter (4 tablespoons), salt and flour and knead 8 minutes until soft and smooth.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
Roll it into an 18 × 12-inch rectangle. Spread with the rest of the soft butter and sprinkle evenly with the brown sugar and cinnamon.
Roll it up tightly from the long side and pinch the seam. Cut into 12 slices (dental floss cuts cleanly) and set them in a greased 9 × 13 pan.
Cover and let rise until puffy and touching, 45 to 60 minutes. (Or refrigerate overnight and let them rise 1 to 1½ hours in the morning.) Heat the oven to 375°F.
Bake 22 to 25 minutes, until golden and the middle roll reads about 190°F.
Stir the powdered sugar, milk and vanilla into a thick glaze and spread it over the warm rolls.

plan.thaw: Thaw, then warm 10 minutes at 300°F.

keeps: Counter: covered, about 2 days; best warm the first day.
Freezer: bake them, cool, and freeze unglazed up to 3 months (University of Missouri’s time for baked yeast rolls); glaze after warming.
recipes.scaling: Each roll is a twelfth of the recipe.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Sweet rolls (Hawaiian-style)
recipes.summary: Soft, slightly sweet pull-apart rolls made with honey, butter and eggs.
steps: Stir the yeast into the warm milk with the honey and sugar and let it stand 5 minutes.
Beat in the eggs, butter and salt, then the flour. Knead 8 to 10 minutes; the dough stays soft.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 to 1½ hours.
Divide into 16 pieces (about 55 g each), round them into tight balls, and set them in rows in a greased 9 × 13 pan.
Let rise until puffy and touching, 45 to 60 minutes. Heat the oven to 350°F.
Bake 20 to 25 minutes, until golden (about 190°F). Brush with melted butter.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter, about 1 hour.

keeps: Counter: in a bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread and rolls).
Freezer: bag them once cool, up to 3 months (University of Missouri).
recipes.scaling: Each roll is a sixteenth of the dough. Many recipes use pineapple juice for part of the milk; this one keeps to pantry staples.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Sourdough starter
recipes.summary: Flour and water, fed daily until wild yeast and bacteria make it bubble and rise: then keep it in the refrigerator for years.

ingredients.prep: about 100 g a day for 2 weeks

equipment: clean glass jar (1 quart) with a loose lid
rubber band to mark the level
steps: Day 1: stir 100 g flour and 100 g lukewarm water in the jar into a thick batter. Cover loosely and leave it in a warm spot for 24 hours.
Day 2: stir it, then keep only 50 g and throw out the rest. Feed it 50 g flour and 50 g water, stir, and mark the level with a rubber band.
Keep feeding once a day the same way (equal weights of starter, flour and water: 1:1:1). When it starts bubbling and smelling yeasty, after about 3 days, feed it twice a day, about every 12 hours.
It’s ready to bake with when it doubles within 4 to 6 hours after a feeding, is bubbly all through, and smells pleasantly sour. That usually takes about 2 weeks (Clemson Extension).
Keeping it: store it in the refrigerator in a clean glass jar with a loose lid, and feed it once a week (Clemson, University of Alaska). Before baking, take it out, feed it, and let it double.
Gray liquid on top is normal (it’s called hooch): stir it back in for a more sour starter, or pour it off.
Throw it out and start over if it turns green (University of Alaska), grows fuzzy mold, or smells rotten rather than sour. When in doubt, throw it out.
Use the starter you remove at each feeding (the discard) in pancakes, waffles or crackers, or throw it away.

stages.do: Feed daily, then twice a day, until it doubles in 4 to 6 hours

keeps: Refrigerator: keep it in a covered glass jar and feed it once a week (Clemson Extension; University of Alaska Extension). Metal containers and spoons aren’t recommended, since the acid can react with the metal (University of Alaska).
recipes.scaling: Keep a small amount (50 to 100 g) and feed it 1:1:1 by weight. To build up starter for baking, feed it 6 to 12 hours before you mix the dough: for example 20 g starter, 50 g flour, 50 g water.
recipes.old_way: In Alaska, “sourdough” also means an old-timer: miners, trappers and homesteaders kept starters going because bread couldn’t be made without them, and supplies came by ship only once or twice a year (University of Alaska Extension).
safety: Use a clean jar, and don’t add baking soda to the starter itself (University of Alaska).
recipes.yield: A jar of active starter; you keep about 50 to 100 g and feed it.

recipes.name: Sourdough bread
recipes.summary: A crusty round loaf raised only with sourdough starter, shaped one day and baked the next.

ingredients.prep: 50 g of it to feed the starter
50 g of it to feed the starter

equipment: bowl or basket lined with a well-floured towel
Dutch oven (5 to 6 quart) with lid
steps: The day before baking, in the morning (6 to 12 hours ahead), feed your starter: 20 g of starter from the jar, 50 g of the flour and 50 g of the water. It’s ready when it has doubled and is bubbly.
Mix all of the risen starter (about 120 g) with the remaining water (about 325 g) and flour (450 g) until no dry flour is left. Cover and rest 1 hour.
Add the salt with a splash of water and squeeze it in. Over the next 2 hours, every 30 minutes, stretch one side of the dough up and fold it over; turn the bowl and repeat 4 times.
Let it rise, covered, until it has grown by about half and has bubbles on the sides, 2 to 4 more hours (longer in a cool kitchen).
In the evening, turn it out, shape it into a tight ball, and set it seam side up in the floured, towel-lined bowl. Cover and refrigerate overnight, 8 to 16 hours.
Next morning, heat the oven to 475°F with the Dutch oven inside for 45 minutes. Turn the cold dough onto parchment, slash the top, and lower it into the pot.
Bake covered 20 minutes, then uncovered 20 to 25 minutes, until very dark brown and about 205°F inside. Cool at least 2 hours before cutting.

stages.do: Feed the starter in the morning
Add the salt, then stretch and fold 4 times
Let it rise until it grows by half
Shape it and chill it overnight
Heat the oven with the pot inside

plan.thaw: Thaw in its wrapping on the counter, then crisp in a 375°F oven 10 minutes.

keeps: Counter: cut side down on a board or in a paper bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread).

Freezer: cool completely, wrap in plastic and then foil or a freezer bag, up to 3 months (University of Missouri). Slice first so you can take out what you need; a whole loaf thaws in its wrapping on the counter in about 3 hours (Cornell).
recipes.scaling: 75% water, 2% salt and about 20% starter by the flour’s weight. Times depend on your starter and your kitchen: go by how the dough looks.
recipes.old_way: Before factory-made yeast went on sale in the United States in the late 1860s, home bakers raised their bread with starters like this one or with yeast from brewing.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
Use oven mitts that cover your wrists for the 475°F pot.
notes: You need an active starter first: see the sourdough starter recipe.

recipes.name: Flour tortillas
recipes.summary: Soft flour tortillas from five pantry staples, cooked in a dry skillet.

ingredients.prep: or lard or shortening, cut in

equipment: heavy skillet or griddle (cast iron is best)
steps: Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt. Stir in the oil (or rub in the lard or shortening with your fingers), then the warm water, and mix to a soft dough.
Knead 2 minutes until smooth. Divide into 10 balls for 8-inch tortillas or 7 for 10-inch. Cover and rest 30 minutes; rested dough rolls out without shrinking.
Heat a dry skillet over medium-high. Roll one ball on a lightly floured counter into a thin round, turning it as you go.
Cook 30 to 60 seconds, until bubbles puff and the underside has brown spots, then flip and cook 30 seconds more.
Stack the cooked tortillas in a folded towel so they steam and stay soft. Roll the next one while each cooks.

stages.do: Mix the dough and let it rest

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter, then warm in a dry skillet.

keeps: Counter: sealed in a bag once cool, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread).
Freezer: stack with parchment between them in a freezer bag, up to about 3 months (the University of Missouri’s time for baked bread).
recipes.scaling: Everything scales by the number of tortillas: each 8-inch tortilla is a tenth of the recipe. Divide the dough by weight for even rounds: about 55 g of dough for 8 inches, 80 g for 10.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Lard gives the flakiest, most traditional tortillas; oil makes them vegan.

recipes.name: Corn tortillas
recipes.summary: Masa harina, water and salt, pressed thin and cooked on a hot griddle.

ingredients.prep: hot from the tap, plus more as needed

equipment: tortilla press, or a heavy skillet and a zip-top bag cut open
steps: Mix the masa harina and salt, then stir in the hot water. Knead in the bowl for a minute: the dough should feel like soft play clay and not crack at the edges when pressed. Add water a spoonful at a time if it cracks, or masa if it sticks.
Cover and rest 15 minutes. Divide into 16 balls about the size of a golf ball (about 34 g), keeping them covered.
Heat a dry griddle over medium-high. Press each ball between two sheets of plastic in a tortilla press (or under a flat-bottomed pan) to about 6 inches across.
Peel off the plastic and cook 30 seconds, flip and cook 45 to 60 seconds, then flip once more for 15 seconds; it often puffs. Keep them warm wrapped in a towel.

stages.do: Mix the dough and let it rest

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag, then reheat in a hot dry skillet until soft.

keeps: Counter: sealed in a bag once cool, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread); they dry out, so reheat them in a skillet.
Freezer: stack with parchment between them in a freezer bag, up to 3 months.
recipes.scaling: Masa and water scale together; the exact water changes with the brand and the weather, so add the last of it by feel.
recipes.old_way: Masa is made by cooking dried corn in water with slaked lime (calcium hydroxide), soaking it, and grinding it. Masa harina is that dough dried into flour. Untreated cornmeal can’t stand in: it won’t form a dough, and the lime treatment also frees the corn’s niacin.
notes: Masa harina is naturally free of wheat, but check the bag if you avoid gluten: some is milled near wheat.

recipes.name: Pita bread
recipes.summary: Rounds of simple dough baked on a hot sheet until they puff into pockets.
equipment: heavy baking sheet or baking stone (or a cast-iron skillet)
steps: Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm water. Add the oil, salt and flour and knead 8 minutes until smooth.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 to 1½ hours.
Heat the oven to 475°F with the baking sheet on the lowest rack for at least 30 minutes.
Divide into 8 balls and rest them 10 minutes, covered. Roll each to a 6-inch round about ¼ inch thick, without creasing.
Bake 2 or 3 at a time on the hot sheet, 3 to 5 minutes, until puffed and just starting to color. (On the stove: cook in a hot dry skillet 1 to 2 minutes per side.)
Stack them in a towel so they stay soft as they cool.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter, about 1 hour.

keeps: Counter: in a bag once cool, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread).
Freezer: bag them, up to 3 months; warm in a skillet or toaster.
recipes.scaling: Each pita is an eighth of the dough (about 75 g).
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Uneven thickness or creases keep them from puffing; they still taste fine as flatbread.

recipes.name: Naan
recipes.summary: A soft yogurt dough cooked in a very hot skillet and brushed with butter.
steps: Stir the yeast and sugar into the warm water and let it stand 5 minutes. Add the yogurt, oil, salt and flour and knead 5 minutes into a soft dough.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1½ hours.
Divide into 8 balls. Roll each into an oval about ¼ inch thick.
Heat the skillet over medium-high until very hot. Cook one naan at a time: when big bubbles form, about 1 minute, flip it, cover the pan, and cook 1 minute more, until charred in spots.
Brush with butter (stir the garlic into the butter for garlic naan) and keep them wrapped in a towel.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter, about 1 hour.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread).
Freezer: with parchment between them, up to 3 months; warm in a skillet.
recipes.scaling: Each naan is an eighth of the dough.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Flatbread (lavash)
recipes.summary: An unleavened dough rolled paper-thin: soft from a skillet for wraps, crisp from the oven for crackers.
steps: Mix the flour and salt, add the oil and water, and knead 5 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
Divide into 8 pieces and roll each as thin as you can, about 10 inches across.
Soft: cook in a hot dry skillet about 1 minute per side, until bubbled with a few brown spots; stack in a towel.
Crisp: bake on a sheet at 400°F 5 to 8 minutes, sprinkled with sesame seeds or salt, until browned; break into crackers.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag.

keeps: Soft: in a bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread); freeze for longer.
Crisp: airtight; crispest within a week or two.
recipes.scaling: Each flatbread is an eighth of the dough.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Biscuits
recipes.summary: Tall, flaky butter biscuits in about 30 minutes, in place of the refrigerated can.

ingredients.prep: very cold, cut in small cubes

steps: Heat the oven to 450°F. Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt in a bowl.
Cut in the cold butter with a pastry blender or your fingertips until the biggest pieces are the size of peas.
Stir in the cold milk with a fork just until the dough comes together; it should look shaggy.
Turn it out on a floured counter, pat it 1 inch thick, fold it in half, and pat it out again. Do this 3 times for flaky layers, ending 1 inch thick.
Cut straight down with a floured cutter (don’t twist) and set the biscuits touching on the baking sheet. Press the scraps together once for the last biscuits.
Bake 12 to 14 minutes, until tall and golden.

stages.do: Mix, fold and cut the biscuits

plan.thaw: Warm frozen biscuits, wrapped in foil, in a 350°F oven about 15 minutes.

keeps: Counter: best warm; in a bag, about 2 days.
Freezer: bake them first, cool, and freeze up to 2 to 3 months; frozen unbaked biscuits come out smaller and less tender (University of Missouri).
recipes.scaling: Everything scales with the flour: 12 g (1 tablespoon) baking powder for every 250 g flour. Cold butter and a hot oven matter more than exact batch size.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Buttermilk biscuits: use ¾ cup buttermilk instead of milk and add ¼ teaspoon baking soda to the flour.

recipes.name: Cornbread
recipes.summary: Cornmeal and flour, lightly sweet, baked in a hot pan in about half an hour.
steps: Heat the oven to 400°F. Grease the pan (for a crisp crust, heat a greased skillet in the oven).
Whisk the cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder and salt. Whisk the milk, egg and melted butter separately, then stir them into the dry mix just until combined.
Pour into the pan and bake 20 to 25 minutes, until golden and a toothpick in the middle comes out clean. Cool 10 minutes.

plan.thaw: Thaw wrapped, then warm in a 350°F oven.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread).
Freezer: wrapped once cool, 2 to 4 months (University of Missouri’s time for quick breads); thaw in the wrapping, 1 to 2 hours.
recipes.scaling: Double it in a 9 × 13 pan; bake 25 to 30 minutes.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Garden flint or dent corn ground to meal works here.

recipes.name: Irish soda bread
recipes.summary: Four ingredients, no yeast: baking soda and buttermilk raise a round loaf in under an hour.

ingredients.prep: plus a little more if dry

steps: Heat the oven to 425°F and flour a baking sheet.
Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt. Pour in the buttermilk and stir with your hand or a spoon just until a soft, shaggy dough forms; don’t knead it.
Turn it out, shape it gently into a round about 2 inches high, and cut a deep cross in the top.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes, until browned and hollow-sounding underneath. Wrap in a towel for a soft crust, or cool on a rack for a crisp one.

plan.thaw: Thaw wrapped; toast slices.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, best within 2 days; it stales faster than yeast bread.
Freezer: wrapped once cool, 2 to 4 months (University of Missouri’s time for quick breads); thaw in the wrapping, 1 to 2 hours.
recipes.scaling: The buttermilk’s acid is what makes the baking soda work: use real buttermilk or the buttermilk stand-in, not plain milk.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Banana bread
recipes.summary: Very ripe bananas, butter and a little brown sugar in a moist loaf.
steps: Heat the oven to 350°F and grease the pan.
Mash the bananas in a bowl, then stir in the melted butter, brown sugar, eggs and vanilla.
Sprinkle the baking soda, salt and cinnamon over the top and stir, then stir in the flour (and nuts) just until no dry flour shows.
Bake 55 to 65 minutes, until a toothpick in the middle comes out clean. Cool 15 minutes in the pan, then on a rack.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the wrapping, 1 to 2 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread).
Freezer: wrapped once cool, 2 to 4 months (University of Missouri’s time for quick breads); thaw in the wrapping, 1 to 2 hours.
recipes.scaling: Double it for two pans. The darker the bananas, the sweeter the bread.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Zucchini bread
recipes.summary: A spiced quick bread that uses up a big garden zucchini.
steps: Heat the oven to 350°F and grease the pan. Grate the zucchini; there’s no need to squeeze it.
Whisk the oil, sugar, eggs and vanilla. Stir in the zucchini.
Sprinkle the baking soda, baking powder, salt and cinnamon over the top and stir, then stir in the flour (and nuts) just until combined.
Bake 50 to 60 minutes, until a toothpick in the middle comes out clean. Cool 15 minutes in the pan, then on a rack.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the wrapping, 1 to 2 hours.

keeps: Counter: wrapped, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread).
Freezer: wrapped once cool, 2 to 4 months (University of Missouri’s time for quick breads); thaw in the wrapping, 1 to 2 hours.
recipes.scaling: A big garden zucchini makes several loaves: about 1½ cups grated per loaf.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Soft pretzels (twists, bites and buns)
recipes.summary: A firm dough shaped into twists, bites or buns, dipped in a hot baking-soda bath and baked deep brown.

ingredients.prep: for the bath: bake it first for a darker crust (see the steps)

equipment: wide stainless-steel or enameled pot (not aluminum)
kitchen gloves (for handling baked baking soda)
steps: For a darker, more traditional crust, bake the baking soda first (you can do this days ahead): spread the ½ cup on a parchment-lined baking sheet and bake at 250°F for 1 hour. Heat turns baking soda into washing soda (sodium carbonate), which is more alkaline; fully changed, it weighs about a third less. Let it cool, then store it in a closed jar labeled “baked baking soda: not for eating”, out of children’s reach. Plain baking soda works too, with a lighter crust.
Dough: stir the yeast and brown sugar into the warm water and let it stand 5 minutes. Add the butter, salt and flour and knead 8 minutes into a smooth, firm dough.
Cover and let it rise until doubled, about 1 hour.

Shape. Twists: divide into 8, roll each into a 24-inch rope, make a U, cross the ends twice, and press them onto the bottom of the U. Buns: 8 tight balls. Bites: roll ropes and cut into 1-inch pieces.
Set them on the parchment-lined sheets and refrigerate, uncovered, 15 to 20 minutes; firm dough holds its shape in the bath. Heat the oven to 425°F.
Bath: in the stainless pot, bring the 8 cups of water to a simmer and stir in ¼ cup of baked baking soda (or ½ cup plain baking soda) a little at a time; it foams. Keep it at a gentle simmer.
Dip 2 or 3 at a time for 20 to 30 seconds (buns 30 seconds a side), lift out with the slotted spoon, drain, and set back on the parchment. Keep children away from the hot pot.
Sprinkle with coarse salt. Slash the buns across the top. Bake twists 12 to 15 minutes, bites 10 to 12, buns 18 to 20, until deep brown.
Let the bath cool, then pour it down the drain with running water.

plan.thaw: Warm frozen pretzels in a 350°F oven 5 to 10 minutes.

keeps: Counter: best the day they’re baked; uncovered or in a paper bag for a day (salt draws moisture in a closed bag).
Freezer: freeze them baked and unsalted, up to 3 months (University of Missouri’s time for baked yeast bread); add salt after warming.
recipes.scaling: Each pretzel or bun is an eighth of the dough (about 105 g). The bath doesn’t scale with the dough: 8 cups of water does a full batch or a half.
recipes.old_way: Southern German bakers dip pretzels and rolls in a weak solution of food-grade lye (sodium hydroxide), which makes the glossy, mahogany crust. Lye is caustic: it burns skin and eyes and attacks aluminum (CDC/NIOSH). Because it needs gloves, eye protection and careful measuring of a hazardous chemical, we describe it here as history only and use baked baking soda at home, which bakers also use in place of lye (Wikipedia).
safety: Don’t taste baked baking soda or the bath, and keep both away from children; store the baked soda in a labeled jar.
Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: The alkaline bath is what browns the crust and gives the pretzel flavor; without it you get a breadstick.
The nutrition numbers leave out the bath, which is poured away.
recipes.yield: 8 large twisted pretzels, 8 pretzel buns, or about 64 bites.

recipes.name: Bagels
recipes.summary: A stiff dough shaped into rings, boiled a minute a side, then baked for a chewy crust.
steps: Stir the yeast and honey into the warm water. Add the flour and salt and knead 10 minutes; the dough is stiff and smooth.
Cover and let it rise until about 1½ times bigger, about 1 hour.
Divide into 8 pieces (about 100 g). Roll each into a 9-inch rope, wrap it around your hand so the ends overlap under your palm, and roll the overlap on the counter to seal. Set them on parchment.
Cover and rest 20 to 30 minutes, until they float when dropped in a bowl of water. (Or refrigerate overnight for more flavor; boil them straight from the fridge.) Heat the oven to 425°F.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil with 1 tablespoon honey. Boil 2 or 3 bagels at a time, 1 minute per side (2 minutes for chewier bagels). Lift out, drain, and add toppings while wet.
Bake 18 to 22 minutes, until deep golden. Cool on a rack at least 20 minutes.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the bag on the counter, about 1 hour.

keeps: Counter: in a paper or plastic bag, about 3 days (NDSU’s figure for bread).
Freezer: slice them first, bag them, up to 3 months (University of Missouri); toast from frozen.
recipes.scaling: Each bagel is an eighth of the dough. Bakeries use barley malt syrup in the water and dough; honey or brown sugar is the home stand-in.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Butter pie crust
recipes.summary: Enough flaky all-butter pastry for one double-crust pie or two single crusts.

ingredients.prep: very cold, cut in ½-inch cubes
ice cold, plus up to 2 tablespoons more

steps: Whisk the flour, salt and sugar. Cut in the cold butter until most of it is pea-sized, with a few bigger flakes.
Sprinkle in the ice water a tablespoon at a time, tossing with a fork, until the dough holds together when you squeeze a handful. Use only as much as you need.
Divide in two, press each half into a flat disk, wrap, and chill at least 1 hour so the butter firms and the flour relaxes.
Roll each disk on a floured counter to a 12-inch round, about ⅛ inch thick, turning it often. Fit it into the pie plate without stretching; fill and bake as your recipe says.

stages.do: Mix the dough and press it into disks

plan.thaw: Thaw wrapped disks in the refrigerator overnight.

keeps: Refrigerator: chill at least 1 hour; well wrapped, it waits overnight.
Freezer: unbaked dough or crusts fitted into pans, 6 to 8 weeks; baked crusts, 2 to 3 months (University of Missouri).
recipes.scaling: Keep the butter about 70% of the flour’s weight. Make it one batch at a time if you mix by hand, so the butter stays cold.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: The salt is low because catalog butter is salted; with unsalted butter, use 1 teaspoon.
recipes.yield: Two 9-inch crusts (one double-crust pie, or two single-crust pies).

recipes.name: Croissants
recipes.summary: A yeast dough folded around a slab of butter three times for flaky layers. A weekend project.

ingredients.prep: 30 g softened for the dough, 280 g cold for the butter block (use unsalted if you have it)

steps: Day 1, evening: mix the flour, yeast, salt, sugar, milk and 30 g soft butter into a smooth dough, about 5 minutes. Pat it into a rectangle, wrap it, and refrigerate overnight.
Day 2: pound and roll the 280 g of cold butter between parchment into a 7-inch square; refrigerate until firm but bendable.
Roll the dough to a 10-inch square, set the butter on it like a diamond, fold the corners over it, and pinch the seams to seal.

Roll it into an 8 × 24-inch strip, fold it in thirds like a letter, wrap, and chill 30 minutes. Do this twice more (three folds in all), chilling 30 minutes after each. If butter breaks through or gets soft, chill longer.
Chill 1 hour, then roll to a 10 × 24-inch rectangle about ¼ inch thick. Cut 12 long triangles (about 4 inches at the base).
Cut a ½-inch notch in the middle of each base, roll each up from the base to the tip, and set them tip-down on the sheets, curved if you like.
Cover loosely and let them rise at cool room temperature (below about 78°F, so the butter stays solid) until puffy and wobbly, 1½ to 2½ hours.
Heat the oven to 400°F. Brush with beaten egg and bake 18 to 22 minutes, until deep golden brown. Cool 20 minutes.

stages.do: Make the butter block and lock it in
Three folds, chilling 30 minutes after each

plan.thaw: Warm frozen baked croissants in a 350°F oven 8 to 10 minutes.

keeps: Counter: best the day they’re baked; in a paper bag up to 2 days, recrisped in the oven.

Freezer: baked, up to 3 months (University of Missouri’s time for baked yeast bread). Shaped, unbaked croissants can be frozen up to about 1 month (NDSU’s time for unbaked rolls); thaw and rise them overnight in the refrigerator, then let them finish rising before baking.
recipes.scaling: About 2 hours of work over 2 days. Keep the butter block 56% of the flour’s weight. A cool kitchen is the main trick: stop and chill whenever the butter softens.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Roll in one direction and keep the edges square; the layers come from the folds, so neat folds bake into neat layers.

recipes.name: Crisp crackers
recipes.summary: Half whole-wheat flour, olive oil and salt, rolled thin and baked crisp.
steps: Heat the oven to 400°F. Mix the flours and salt, add the oil and water, and knead briefly into a smooth, firm dough. Rest 10 minutes.
Divide in half. Roll each half on parchment as thin as you can, about 1/16 inch. Slide the parchment onto a baking sheet.
Prick all over with a fork, cut into 2-inch squares with the pizza cutter (no need to separate them), and sprinkle with coarse salt and seeds.
Bake 12 to 16 minutes, until browned and crisp; edges brown first, so take those off early if needed. Cool on the pan, then break apart.
keeps: Pantry: airtight once completely cool. NDSU gives opened crackers about 1 month; homemade ones are crispest within the first week or two.
recipes.scaling: Thinner dough makes crisper crackers; thick spots stay soft, so roll evenly.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
notes: Discard from a sourdough starter can replace up to half the water and some flour.
recipes.yield: About 10 oz of crackers (about 60 two-inch squares).

recipes.name: Fresh egg pasta
recipes.summary: Flour and eggs, rolled by hand and cut into fettuccine, spaghetti-style strands or lasagna sheets.

makes.label: g of dried pasta it stands in for
g of dried lasagna noodles it stands in for

ingredients.prep: only if the dough is dry

equipment: rolling pin (a long, thin one is easiest)
steps: Mound the flour on the counter with the salt and make a wide well in the middle. Crack the eggs into the well and beat them with a fork, pulling in flour from the inside wall a little at a time.
When it gets too thick to stir, push it together with your hands. Knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and firm, like modeling clay. Add water a few drops at a time only if it won’t come together.
Wrap it and rest 30 minutes at room temperature so it rolls out easily.

Cut the dough in quarters; keep the others wrapped. On a lightly floured counter roll one piece from the center outward, turning it often, until it is thin enough to see your hand through, about 1/16 inch.
Fettuccine: dust the sheet with flour, roll it up loosely into a flat log, and slice it ¼ inch wide. Shake out the strands.

Spaghetti-style: roll the sheet a little thicker (about ⅛ inch) and cut ⅛-inch strips. They come out square-edged, like the pasta Italian cooks cut on a wire frame; perfectly round spaghetti needs an extruder.
Lasagna sheets: cut the rolled sheet into rectangles to fit your pan, about 4 × 12 inches for a 9 × 13. Boil them 1 minute, or layer them in unboiled when the sauce is on the loose side.
Cook fresh pasta in plenty of boiling salted water 2 to 4 minutes, until tender with a little bite.

plan.thaw: Cook it straight from frozen.

keeps: Refrigerator: cook it right away, or refrigerate it covered up to 3 days. Don’t leave it drying at room temperature more than 2 hours (Iowa State Extension).
Freezer: dust with flour, make loose nests, freeze on a tray, then bag them, for 3 to 6 months. Cook straight from frozen, a minute or two longer.
recipes.scaling: Use 100 g (about ¾ cup) flour per large egg and scale by whole eggs: 2 eggs for about ½ lb of dried-pasta’s worth, 4 eggs for about 1 lb. Don’t scale rolling by hand much past 4 eggs at once; roll in batches.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
Raw egg dough is a raw food until it is cooked; cooking is the step that makes it safe (Iowa State Extension).
recipes.yield: About 1 lb of fresh pasta, which stands in for about ¾ lb of dried (fresh pasta holds more water). Serves 4 as a main dish.

recipes.name: Egg noodles
recipes.summary: Thick, tender egg noodles for chicken noodle soup and buttered noodles.

makes.label: g of dried egg noodles they stand in for

steps: Beat the eggs, milk and salt in a bowl. Stir in the flour to make a stiff dough.
Knead on a floured counter about 5 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest 20 minutes.
Roll it out about ⅛ inch thick. Let the sheet air-dry 20 to 30 minutes, turning once, until it feels leathery but still bends.
Dust with flour, roll it up loosely, and cut ¼-inch strips (or wider, if you like them that way). Shake them apart.
Cook in boiling salted water or simmering broth until tender, 4 to 8 minutes depending on thickness.

stages.do: Mix, knead and rest the dough
Roll, dry and cut the noodles

plan.thaw: Cook them straight from frozen.

keeps: Refrigerator: cook it right away, or refrigerate it covered up to 3 days. Don’t leave it drying at room temperature more than 2 hours (Iowa State Extension).
Freezer: dust with flour, make loose nests, freeze on a tray, then bag them, for 3 to 6 months. Cook straight from frozen, a minute or two longer.
recipes.scaling: Scale by whole eggs: each egg goes with about 125 g (1 cup) of flour and 2 tablespoons of milk.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
The drying time on the counter is part of the 2-hour limit for raw egg dough (Iowa State Extension).
recipes.yield: About 14 oz of fresh noodles, which stands in for about 9 oz of dried egg noodles (about 6 cups dry).

recipes.name: Butter (and the buttermilk it leaves)
recipes.summary: Whip cream past whipped cream until it breaks into butter and a thin, sweet buttermilk.

makes.label: g of butter (about 2 sticks is 226 g)

ingredients.prep: not ultra-pasteurized if you can find it; it churns faster

equipment: stand mixer with whisk, hand mixer, or a 1-quart jar with a tight lid
steps: Let the cream sit out about 20 minutes so it is cool but not fridge-cold, about 55 to 60°F.

Whip it on medium-high. It turns to whipped cream, then stiff and grainy, then suddenly breaks: yellow clumps and splashing thin liquid, usually 8 to 12 minutes. Drape a towel over the mixer once it starts to splash. (Or shake it hard in the jar, 10 to 20 minutes.)
Pour everything into a strainer over a bowl. The liquid is the buttermilk; save it in the fridge.

Wash the butter: put it in a bowl, add about ½ cup ice water, and press and fold it with a spatula, then pour the cloudy water off. Repeat until the water stays clear, usually 3 or 4 times. Leftover buttermilk is what makes butter go sour.
Knead in the salt if you are using it, press out the last of the water, shape it, wrap it and refrigerate.

stages.do: Churn, wash and shape the butter

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator.

keeps: Refrigerator: 1 to 2 months, wrapped (NDSU’s figure for butter); homemade butter lasts longest when every bit of buttermilk is washed out.
Freezer: 6 to 9 months (NDSU). Unsalted butter loses flavor sooner (NDSU).
The buttermilk: keep it cold and use it within about 5 days, as for milk (NDSU).
recipes.scaling: Each pint of cream makes about 7½ oz of butter. Churn no more than the mixer bowl can hold at one-third full, since cream more than doubles before it breaks.
recipes.old_way: On farms, cream was skimmed from milk, often allowed to sour a little, and churned by hand in a wooden churn. The thin liquid left behind was the original buttermilk; today’s thick store buttermilk is made instead by adding cultures to milk.
notes: The buttermilk from churning sweet cream is thin and mild, not the tangy cultured buttermilk sold in stores. Use it like milk in pancakes, biscuits or bread. In a recipe that counts on buttermilk’s acid to work with baking soda, it won’t do the same job.

nutrition.why: Most of the cream’s water, sugar and some protein leave with the buttermilk, so the numbers are USDA’s for butter.

recipes.yield: About 7½ oz of butter (a little under 2 sticks) and about 1 cup of buttermilk from 1 pint of cream.

recipes.name: Whipped cream
recipes.summary: One cup of cream, a little sugar and vanilla, whipped to soft peaks in a few minutes.
steps: Chill the bowl and whisk (or beaters) for 10 minutes if you can.
Beat the cold cream with the sugar and vanilla on medium-high until it holds soft peaks that droop at the tip, 2 to 4 minutes.
Stop there for spooning; beat a little longer for firmer peaks to pipe. Past that it turns grainy and heads toward butter.

plan.thaw: Frozen dollops can go straight onto a warm dessert or into cocoa.

keeps: Refrigerator: best within a few hours; covered, it holds about a day before it weeps (whisk it a few strokes to bring it back).
Freezer: pipe or spoon sweetened mounds onto a tray, freeze, then bag them (NDSU).
recipes.scaling: One cup of cream makes about 2 cups whipped (USU). Whip up to 2 cups of cream at once with a hand mixer; more fits a stand mixer.

recipes.name: Plain yogurt
recipes.summary: A quart of milk and a few spoonfuls of yogurt with live cultures, kept warm for 6 to 8 hours.

ingredients.prep: plain, with live active cultures (store-bought or from your last batch)

equipment: clean jars or a bowl with a lid
a warm spot: oven with the light on, a cooler with warm water, or a multicooker’s yogurt setting
steps: Heat the milk in a heavy pot over medium, stirring often, to 180°F. Hold it near 180°F for 10 minutes for thinner yogurt or 20 for thicker, stirring.
Cool it to 108 to 112°F; set the pot in a sink of cold water to speed it up.
Stir a little warm milk into the starter yogurt, then stir that back into the pot. Pour into clean jars and cover.
Keep it at 108 to 112°F, undisturbed, 6 to 8 hours, until it sets like soft custard.
Refrigerate it as soon as it sets; chilling stops it from getting more sour. It firms up as it chills.
Save 3 tablespoons to start the next batch within 5 to 7 days. After 5 or 6 batches, start again with fresh store-bought yogurt.

stages.do: Cool the milk and stir in the starter

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator; stir well (it turns a little grainy).

keeps: Refrigerator: 1 to 2 weeks (NDSU); WSU Extension gives 10 to 21 days for yogurt made with care.
Freezer: 1 to 2 months (NDSU); it turns grainy, so use thawed yogurt in smoothies and baking.
recipes.scaling: Use 2 to 3 teaspoons of starter per cup of milk (WSU). More starter doesn’t make it set faster; it can make it sour.
safety: Use pasteurized milk and very clean jars and spoons (WSU).
notes: For thicker yogurt, stir some nonfat dry milk powder into the cold milk before heating (WSU).

recipes.name: Greek-style yogurt
recipes.summary: Homemade yogurt strained in the refrigerator until thick.
equipment: strainer lined with a coffee filter or a double layer of cheesecloth
steps: Make plain yogurt (heat the milk to 180°F, cool to 108 to 112°F, stir in the starter, keep warm 6 to 8 hours until set, then chill).
Spoon the cold yogurt into the lined strainer set over a bowl, cover, and refrigerate.
Strain 2 to 4 hours for thick yogurt, or overnight for something close to soft cheese. Spoon it into a container; the whey can replace water in bread.

stages.do: Cool the milk and stir in the starter
Chill, then strain in the refrigerator

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator and stir.

keeps: Refrigerator: 1 to 2 weeks, like plain yogurt (NDSU).
Freezer: 1 to 2 months; it turns grainy (NDSU).
recipes.scaling: Straining halves the volume, so make twice as much plain yogurt as the thick yogurt you need.
safety: Strain it in the refrigerator, not on the counter.

nutrition.why: Straining pours off whey (water, some sugar and minerals), so the numbers are USDA’s for plain Greek yogurt.

recipes.yield: About 2 cups thick yogurt (and about 2 cups of whey) from 1 quart of milk.

recipes.name: Fresh ricotta-style cheese
recipes.summary: Hot milk and cream curdled with lemon juice and drained: soft, fresh cheese in under an hour.
equipment: strainer lined with a double layer of cheesecloth
steps: Heat the milk, cream and salt in a heavy pot over medium, stirring often so the bottom doesn’t scorch, to 185 to 190°F (steaming, with small bubbles at the edge).

Take it off the heat. Pour in the lemon juice and stir gently just two or three times. Curds should separate from the yellowish whey within a minute; if it still looks milky, stir in another tablespoon of lemon juice.
Let it stand 10 minutes without stirring.
Ladle the curds into the lined strainer set over a bowl. Drain 10 to 15 minutes for soft, creamy cheese or 30 to 60 minutes for a firmer one to use in lasagna.
Refrigerate it in a covered container right away.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator and drain; it turns crumbly, so cook with it.

keeps: Refrigerator: about 1 week (NDSU’s figure for ricotta).
Freezer: about 1 month; the texture turns crumbly, fine for baked dishes (NDSU).
recipes.scaling: Scale the milk, cream and lemon together. Ultra-pasteurized milk forms weak, small curds, so use regular pasteurized milk.
safety: Use pasteurized milk and very clean equipment; fresh cheeses are watched for Listeria and other germs, which sanitation and proper heating control (NMSU).
notes: Without the cream it still works, with smaller, firmer curds and about 1½ cups of cheese.

nutrition.why: Much of the milk’s water and sugar drains off with the whey, so the numbers are USDA’s for whole-milk ricotta.

recipes.yield: About 2 cups (about 1 lb), depending on how long it drains.

recipes.name: Chicken stock
recipes.summary: Chicken wings or saved bones simmered slowly with vegetables: about 3 quarts.

ingredients.prep: or backs and necks, or the bones of 2 roast chickens

steps: Put the chicken in the pot with the cold water. Bring it slowly just to a boil over medium heat, then turn it down to the barest simmer. Skim off the gray foam for the first 15 minutes.
Add the vegetables and herbs. Simmer uncovered 3 to 4 hours, with only a bubble or two breaking the surface; add water if the bones peek out.
Strain it, pressing lightly on the solids, and throw the solids away.
Cool it quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours. The next day, lift off the fat that hardens on top.
Leave it unsalted and salt the dish you use it in.

stages.do: Start the stock and skim it
Strain and cool in shallow containers

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator, then bring to a rolling boil.

keeps: Refrigerator: 1 to 2 days (the University of Minnesota’s figure for meat broth; NDSU allows 3 to 4), so freeze what you won’t use soon.
Freezer: 2 to 3 months (University of Minnesota). Freeze it in 1- and 2-cup containers, leaving room for it to expand.
recipes.scaling: Scale the chicken, vegetables and water together; keep the water just covering the bones. A double batch needs a 12- to 16-quart pot and the same simmering time.
safety: Cool it fast: divide it into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking (USDA).
Bring stock to a rolling boil when you reheat it (USDA).
notes: Save the bones from a roast chicken in the freezer until you have enough for a pot.

nutrition.why: Most of the chicken and vegetables are strained out, so the numbers are USDA’s for home-made chicken stock (USDA’s version has a little salt; unsalted stock has less sodium).

recipes.name: Beef stock
recipes.summary: Roasted beef bones simmered for hours into a rich, brown stock.
steps: Heat the oven to 425°F. Roast the bones in a single layer 30 minutes. Add the onion, carrots and celery, smear the tomato paste over the bones, and roast 15 minutes more, until well browned.
Move everything to the pot. Pour a cup of the water into the hot pan, scrape up the browned bits, and add it to the pot with the rest of the water and the herbs.
Bring it just to a boil, skim, and simmer uncovered at the barest bubble 5 to 6 hours, adding water to keep the bones covered.
Strain, cool quickly in shallow containers, and refrigerate within 2 hours. Lift off the fat once it hardens.

stages.do: Start the stock and skim it
Strain and cool in shallow containers

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator, then bring to a rolling boil.

keeps: Refrigerator: 1 to 2 days (the University of Minnesota’s figure for meat broth; NDSU allows 3 to 4).
Freezer: 2 to 3 months (University of Minnesota).
recipes.scaling: Scale the bones and water together; the simmering time stays the same.
safety: Cool it fast: divide it into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking (USDA).
Bring stock to a rolling boil when you reheat it (USDA).

nutrition.why: The bones and vegetables are strained out, so the numbers are USDA’s for home-made beef stock.

recipes.name: Vegetable stock
recipes.summary: Onions, carrots, celery, mushrooms and herbs, simmered an hour.
steps: Warm the oil in a large pot over medium. Cook the onions, carrots, celery and mushrooms, stirring now and then, until they soften and brown a little, about 10 minutes.
Add the garlic, herbs and water. Bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered 1 hour.
Strain, pressing on the vegetables to get all the liquid. Cool in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator, then bring to a boil.

keeps: Refrigerator: 3 to 4 days, as for soups (FoodSafety.gov).
Freezer: 2 to 3 months (FoodSafety.gov).
recipes.scaling: Scale the vegetables and water together; keep the simmer at 1 hour (longer can turn it bitter).
safety: Cool it fast: divide it into shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking (USDA).
Bring stock to a rolling boil when you reheat it (USDA).
notes: Onion skins add color; strong vegetables like cabbage and broccoli take over the flavor, so leave them out.

nutrition.why: The vegetables are strained out, so the numbers are USDA’s for vegetable broth; yours has much less sodium unless you salt it.

recipes.name: Tomato sauce from fresh tomatoes
recipes.summary: Ripe tomatoes cooked down into plain sauce: a good use for a garden full of them.

ingredients.prep: or any ripe tomatoes; paste types cook down fastest

equipment: food mill, or a sieve and spoon
steps: Wash the tomatoes, cut out the cores, and quarter them.
Simmer them covered in a wide pot, stirring, until they collapse and turn juicy, about 15 minutes.
Press them through a food mill or sieve to remove the skins and seeds.
Return the purée to the pot and boil it gently, uncovered, stirring often and more as it thickens, until the volume drops by about a third (thin sauce, 1 to 1½ hours) or by half (thick sauce).
Salt it if you like. Cool in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator.

keeps: Refrigerator: 3 to 5 days (NDSU’s figure for tomato-based sauce).
Freezer: leave ½ inch of space in a wide-mouth pint container (1 inch in a quart) and freeze up to 8 to 12 months for best quality (NCHFP’s figure for frozen fruits and vegetables).
recipes.scaling: Plan on about 5 lb of tomatoes per quart of thin sauce and 6½ lb per quart of thick sauce (NCHFP). A wider pot cooks it down faster than a tall one; the time depends on the pot, not just the amount.
safety: This recipe is for the refrigerator and freezer. To can tomato sauce, use NCHFP’s tested Standard Tomato Sauce, which adds acid; don’t can this one.
