nutrition.why: The skins and seeds stay in the food mill, so the numbers are USDA’s for unsalted tomato purée, the closest match.
nutrition.description: Tomato products, canned, puree, without salt added

recipes.yield: About 1 quart (4 cups) of thin sauce, like canned tomato sauce. Cook it down to half for a thick sauce (about 3 cups).

recipes.name: Marinara and pizza sauce
recipes.summary: A 20-minute sauce from a can of crushed tomatoes, garlic and herbs, about a jar’s worth.
steps: Warm the oil in a saucepan over medium-low. Cook the onion, if using, until soft, about 5 minutes; add the garlic and cook 1 minute without letting it brown.
Stir in the tomatoes, herbs, salt and pepper flakes. Simmer, partly covered and stirring now and then, 20 minutes. Taste for salt.
Pizza sauce: skip the onion and the simmering. Stir the crushed tomatoes with the oil, garlic, herbs and salt and spread it on the raw dough; it cooks on the pizza.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator.

keeps: Refrigerator: 3 to 5 days (NDSU’s figure for tomato-based sauce).
Freezer: 2 to 3 months for best quality (FoodSafety.gov’s time for soups and stews, the closest entry). Frozen food kept at 0°F stays safe longer; it just loses quality.
recipes.scaling: Scale by cans of tomatoes. A double batch takes a few minutes longer to simmer down.
notes: From the garden: about 3 lb of fresh, ripe tomatoes, peeled and chopped, can replace the can; simmer 30 to 40 minutes longer.

recipes.name: Fresh tomato salsa
recipes.summary: Chopped ripe tomatoes, onion, jalapeño, cilantro and lime: about 3 cups.
equipment: rubber or plastic gloves for the jalapeño
steps: Wash the vegetables and herbs under running water.
Wear gloves to seed and mince the jalapeño, and don’t touch your eyes.
Stir everything together in a bowl. Let it stand 15 minutes, taste, and add more lime or salt as you like. Drain off extra juice before serving if it’s very wet.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator and drain the extra liquid.

keeps: Refrigerator: keep it cold; Iowa State Extension allows up to 2 weeks for fresh salsa, and Ohio State says “a couple of weeks.” It’s best in the first few days.
Freezer: the only safe way to keep a home salsa recipe long-term; thawed, it is watery, so drain it (Iowa State).
recipes.scaling: Scales evenly. Add the jalapeño and lime a little at a time in big batches, since peppers vary a lot in heat.
safety: Don’t can this salsa: only tested recipes like NCHFP’s are safe to can.

recipes.name: Refrigerator dill pickles
recipes.summary: Cucumber slices in a hot vinegar brine with dill and garlic, kept in the fridge: no canning.

ingredients.prep: firm, sliced ¼ inch thick (about 3 cups); pickling cucumbers are best
pickling salt if you have it

steps: Wash the jar and lid in hot soapy water and rinse well, then sterilize the jar by boiling it 10 minutes, as UW Extension advises for refrigerator pickles.
Heat the vinegar, water, salt and sugar until it simmers, stirring until they dissolve. Take it off the heat.
Put the dill, garlic and pepper flakes in the jar. Pack the cucumber slices in closely, leaving about ½ inch at the top.
Pour in the warm brine to cover the cucumbers. Close the jar and refrigerate.
Wait 1 to 3 days for the flavor to develop before eating. Keep them in the refrigerator.

stages.do: Slice, pack and pour the brine

keeps: Refrigerator: up to 1 month (UW Extension); Oregon State’s recipe allows up to 3 months.
Don’t freeze: they turn soft.
recipes.scaling: Keep the vinegar-to-water ratio exactly as written (2 to 1): don’t cut the vinegar, and use vinegar labeled 5% acidity (UW Extension, NDSU). Scale by jars.
safety: These are not canned and must stay refrigerated. For shelf-stable pickles, use a tested recipe from NCHFP.
notes: Table salt works, but its additives can cloud the brine; pickling salt keeps it clear (UW Extension).

nutrition.why: Much of the brine’s salt stays in the jar, so the numbers are USDA’s for dill pickles; this recipe’s pickles are likely lower in sodium.

recipes.yield: One quart jar (about ¾ lb of pickles).

recipes.name: Mayonnaise
recipes.summary: Pasteurized egg, lemon, mustard and oil, blended in under a minute.
equipment: immersion blender and a tall jar that just fits it, or a bowl and whisk
steps: Use pasteurized eggs: mayonnaise is eaten raw, and FDA and USDA advise pasteurized eggs for anything served with raw egg.

Immersion blender: put the egg, lemon juice, mustard and salt in the jar and pour the oil on top. Set the blender on the bottom, run it, and slowly lift it as the mayonnaise thickens, about 30 seconds.
By hand: whisk the egg, lemon, mustard and salt, then whisk in the oil a few drops at a time until it thickens, then in a thin stream.
Taste and add lemon or salt. Refrigerate right away.
keeps: Refrigerator: no agency publishes a time for homemade mayonnaise. We go by USDA’s nearest entries, raw egg yolks and homemade eggnog: 2 to 4 days.
Don’t freeze it; it separates.
recipes.scaling: One egg holds up to about 1 cup of oil; make one batch at a time.
safety: Use pasteurized shell eggs (FDA, USDA). Refrigerate it right away and don’t leave it out more than 2 hours (USDA).

recipes.name: Ranch dressing
recipes.summary: Buttermilk, mayonnaise and sour cream with dried herbs: dressing or dip.
equipment: bowl and whisk, or a jar
steps: Whisk everything together.
Chill at least 30 minutes so the dried herbs soften and flavor it.
For a dip, use half the buttermilk; for a thinner dressing, add a little more.
keeps: Refrigerator: use it within a few days and by the earliest date on the dairy you used; NDSU’s figure for homemade dips is 2 days.
Don’t freeze it.
recipes.scaling: Scales evenly.
notes: Uses store or homemade mayonnaise.

recipes.name: Italian-style vinaigrette
recipes.summary: Three parts oil to one part vinegar, shaken with mustard, garlic and herbs.
steps: Put everything in the jar, close it, and shake hard until it looks creamy.
Taste on a leaf of lettuce and add salt or vinegar. Shake again just before using.
keeps: Refrigerator: use within 4 days. Garlic and herbs in oil can grow the germ that causes botulism, so Oregon State Extension says to keep any homemade oil with garlic or herbs, fresh or dried, cold and use it within 4 days.
Olive oil firms up in the fridge: let it stand 10 minutes and shake.
recipes.scaling: Keep the 3-to-1 oil-to-vinegar ratio; scale everything else with it.
safety: Keep it refrigerated and use it within 4 days (Oregon State Extension).

recipes.name: Dry breadcrumbs
recipes.summary: Day-old bread dried in a low oven and ground: the plain crumbs for meatloaf and breading.

ingredients.prep: day-old is best; any bread or crusts work

equipment: food processor or blender (or a zip-top bag and rolling pin)
steps: Heat the oven to 300°F. Tear the bread into pieces and spread them on a baking sheet.
Bake 15 to 25 minutes, stirring once, until completely dry and crisp all the way through and only lightly golden.
Cool, then grind in a food processor or blender, or crush in a bag with a rolling pin. Sift out big pieces for fine crumbs.
Italian-style: stir in 1 teaspoon Italian seasoning and ¼ teaspoon garlic powder.

plan.thaw: Use straight from the freezer.

keeps: Pantry: airtight once completely cool. NDSU gives dried bread crumbs about 6 months; if yours aren’t bone-dry, freeze them instead.
Freezer: in a bag, use straight from the freezer.
recipes.scaling: 8 slices of sandwich bread make about 1⅓ cups. Dry them in a single layer; crowded crumbs steam instead of drying.
notes: Uses store or homemade bread; the planner counts the slices.

recipes.name: Panko-style crumbs
recipes.summary: Crustless white bread pulsed into coarse flakes and dried without browning, for a light, crisp coating.
equipment: food processor, or the large holes of a box grater
steps: Heat the oven to 300°F. Pulse the crustless bread in a food processor into coarse flakes (or grate it).
Spread them on a baking sheet and bake 8 to 12 minutes, stirring once, until dry but still pale.
Cool completely before storing.

plan.thaw: Use straight from the freezer.

keeps: Pantry: airtight once completely dry (NDSU gives dried bread crumbs about 6 months); freeze them if you’re not sure.
recipes.scaling: 8 slices make about 2 cups of flakes.
notes: Save the crusts for dry breadcrumbs.

recipes.name: Croutons
recipes.summary: Cubes of bread tossed with olive oil and seasoning, baked crisp.

ingredients.prep: or any day-old bread, in ¾-inch cubes

steps: Heat the oven to 375°F. Toss the bread cubes with the oil, seasoning, garlic powder and salt.
Spread them in one layer and bake 12 to 15 minutes, stirring once, until golden and crisp. They crisp more as they cool.

plan.thaw: Use from the freezer; crisp them a few minutes in the oven.

keeps: Pantry: airtight, about 1 week for the best crunch; the oil goes stale after that.
Freezer: in a bag; recrisp in a 350°F oven for a few minutes.
recipes.scaling: Scales evenly; use two baking sheets for a double batch so they toast instead of steam.

recipes.name: Pancake and waffle mix
recipes.summary: A jar of dry mix for quick pancakes or waffles: add an egg, milk and butter.
steps: Whisk everything together very well, so the baking powder is spread evenly. Store airtight, labeled with the date and the directions below.

Pancakes: whisk 1 cup mix with 1 egg, ¾ cup milk and 2 tablespoons melted butter or oil, just until no dry flour remains (a few lumps are fine). Cook ¼-cup scoops on a greased griddle over medium heat, flipping when bubbles pop on top.
Waffles: 1 cup mix, 1 egg, ¾ cup milk and 3 tablespoons melted butter, in a hot waffle iron.
Buttermilk pancakes: use buttermilk instead of milk and add ¼ teaspoon baking soda per cup of mix.
keeps: Pantry: airtight in a cool, dry place. Use it within about 3 months, because opened baking powder loses strength in 3 to 6 months (NDSU).
recipes.scaling: Each cup of flour takes 2 teaspoons baking powder and ½ teaspoon salt; scale by the cup.
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).
recipes.yield: About 5 cups of mix, enough for 5 batches of about eight 4-inch pancakes.

recipes.name: Granola
recipes.summary: Oats, nuts, honey and a little oil baked slow until golden, with raisins stirred in after.
equipment: rimmed baking sheet lined with parchment
steps: Heat the oven to 300°F. Stir the oats, nuts, cinnamon and salt in a large bowl.
Warm the honey and oil together until runny, stir in the vanilla, and pour it over the oats. Mix until everything is coated.
Spread it on the lined sheet and press it flat with a spatula.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes, turning the pan halfway, until golden. For clusters, don’t stir; for loose granola, stir every 15 minutes.
Cool completely on the pan (it crisps as it cools), then break it up and stir in the raisins.

plan.thaw: Use straight from the freezer.

keeps: Pantry: airtight, about 2 weeks for the best crunch.
Freezer: in a bag for longer.
recipes.scaling: Scales evenly; bake a double batch on two sheets, switching racks halfway.
safety: Honey is not for babies under 12 months old.

recipes.name: Applesauce
recipes.summary: Apples simmered soft and mashed, sweetened only if you like.

ingredients.prep: about 7 medium, a mix of sweet and tart

equipment: potato masher, food mill or blender
steps: Peel, core and slice the apples (or leave the peels on if you’ll press the sauce through a food mill).
Put them in the pot with the water and lemon juice, cover, and simmer, stirring now and then, until very soft, 15 to 20 minutes.
Mash for chunky sauce, or purée or press through a food mill for smooth. Stir in cinnamon and sugar to taste, if using.
Cool in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours.

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator.

keeps: Refrigerator: about 5 to 7 days (NDSU’s figure for opened canned fruit, the closest entry it has).
Freezer: leave ½ inch of space in a wide-mouth pint container (1 inch in a quart) and freeze up to 8 to 12 months for best quality (NCHFP).
recipes.scaling: Plan on about 3 lb of apples per quart (NCHFP’s average). Tart apples make a tangier sauce; 1 to 2 lb of tart apples per 3 lb of sweet ones balances it.
safety: To can applesauce, follow NCHFP’s tested recipe; this one is for the refrigerator and freezer.

nutrition.why: The peels and cores are left behind, so the numbers are USDA’s for unsweetened applesauce (sugar, if you add it, isn’t counted).

recipes.yield: About 1 quart (4 cups) from 3 lb of apples.

recipes.name: Simple syrup
recipes.summary: Equal parts sugar and water, for lemonade and iced tea.
steps: Heat the sugar and water, stirring, just until the sugar dissolves and the syrup is clear. It doesn’t need to boil.
Cool and pour into a clean jar. For a richer syrup, use 2 parts sugar to 1 part water.
keeps: Refrigerator: covered, in a clean jar. We didn’t find a published storage time for it, so make small batches and throw it out if it turns cloudy or grows mold.
recipes.scaling: Scales evenly.

recipes.name: Taco seasoning
recipes.summary: The packet’s worth of chili powder, cumin, paprika, garlic, onion and oregano, without fillers.
steps: Stir everything together.
To use: brown 1 lb of meat, drain, then stir in the seasoning with ⅔ cup water and simmer until thick, about 5 minutes.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, away from heat and light, about 6 months (NDSU’s figure for herb and spice blends).
recipes.scaling: Scales evenly. Mix a big jar and use 3 tablespoons per pound of meat.
notes: Chili powder is itself a blend that varies by brand; adjust the cayenne to your family.
recipes.yield: About 3 tablespoons, the same job as one 1-oz packet: seasons 1 lb of meat.

recipes.name: Chili seasoning
recipes.summary: A blend for a pot of chili made with 2 lb of meat or beans.
steps: Stir everything together.
Add it with the tomatoes and simmer the chili at least 30 minutes so the spices mellow.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, away from heat and light, about 6 months (NDSU’s figure for herb and spice blends).
recipes.scaling: Scales evenly.
recipes.yield: About ⅓ cup: one pot of chili (2 lb of meat or 4 cans of beans).

recipes.name: Italian seasoning
recipes.summary: Dried oregano, basil, thyme and rosemary in one jar.
steps: Crush the rosemary between your fingers or in a mortar, then stir everything together.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, away from heat and light, about 6 months (NDSU’s figure for herb and spice blends).
recipes.scaling: Scales evenly. Dried herbs from your own garden work well here.

recipes.name: Powdered sugar
recipes.summary: Granulated sugar and a spoonful of cornstarch, ground fine in a blender.
steps: Blend the sugar and cornstarch on high 1 to 2 minutes, until fine as flour.
Let the dust settle a minute before you open the lid. Sift before using in frosting.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, like any sugar (NDSU gives sugars 18 to 24 months).
recipes.scaling: Store powdered sugar has 2 to 5% starch to keep it from caking (Wikipedia); a tablespoon per cup of sugar is about 4%. It comes out a little less fine than store powdered sugar.
notes: For whipped cream and dusting, granulated sugar ground alone works too.

recipes.name: Brown sugar
recipes.summary: White sugar with a little molasses worked in: light or dark.

ingredients.prep: for dark brown; use 1½ teaspoons for light

equipment: bowl and fork, or a mixer
steps: Work the molasses into the sugar with a fork (or a mixer on low) until the color is even and there are no streaks.
keeps: Pantry: airtight, or it dries out and hardens (NDSU gives sugars 18 to 24 months).
recipes.scaling: Store brown sugar is white sugar with molasses added: about 3.5% molasses for light and 6.5% for dark, by volume (Wikipedia). That is about 1½ teaspoons (light) or 1 tablespoon (dark) per cup. NDSU’s chart uses ¼ cup molasses per cup of sugar, which makes a much darker, wetter sugar.
notes: In a pinch, plain white sugar also works cup for cup (USU, Missouri), with less caramel flavor.

recipes.name: Self-rising flour
recipes.summary: All-purpose flour with the baking powder and salt already in it.
steps: Whisk the flour, baking powder and salt together very well.
keeps: Mix it as you need it: it lasts only as long as the baking powder, which loses strength 3 to 6 months after opening (NDSU).
recipes.scaling: Per cup: 1 cup minus 2 teaspoons all-purpose flour, 1½ teaspoons baking powder and ½ teaspoon salt (NDSU and University of Missouri; Colorado State uses 1¼ teaspoons baking powder and ¼ teaspoon salt).
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Cake flour
recipes.summary: Less all-purpose flour, sifted, for a tender cake.
steps: For each cup of cake flour, measure 1 cup minus 2 tablespoons of all-purpose flour and sift it.
keeps: Pantry: as for flour (NDSU: 6 to 8 months once opened).
recipes.scaling: 1 cup cake flour = 1 cup minus 2 tablespoons all-purpose (NDSU, Missouri, Colorado State).
safety: Don’t taste raw dough or batter, and wash your hands and the counter after handling flour: raw flour can carry germs that only baking kills (FDA).

recipes.name: Buttermilk stand-in
recipes.summary: Milk soured with lemon juice or vinegar, for baking when you’re out of buttermilk.

ingredients.prep: enough to make 1 cup with the lemon

steps: Put the lemon juice in a measuring cup and add milk to the 1-cup line.
Stir and let it stand 5 to 10 minutes, until slightly thickened.
keeps: Use it right away, in the recipe.
recipes.scaling: 1 tablespoon lemon juice or vinegar per cup (NDSU, Missouri, Colorado State, USU). Plain yogurt also stands in cup for cup (Missouri).
notes: It works in pancakes, biscuits and cakes, where the acid reacts with baking soda. It’s thinner than cultured buttermilk.

recipes.name: Black beans from dry
recipes.summary: A pound of dried beans soaked and simmered: about as much as four cans, for a fraction of the cost.

ingredients.prep: about 10 cups to soak and 10 to cook

steps: Spread the beans on a tray and pick out any small stones or shriveled beans, then rinse them.
Soak them in plenty of cold water (about 10 cups) at least 5 hours or overnight.

Drain and rinse. Cover with fresh water by about 2 inches, add the bay leaf, and bring to a boil. Boil hard for at least 30 minutes: soaking and then boiling in fresh water for at least 30 minutes destroys a natural toxin in raw beans, especially kidney beans (FDA).
Turn the heat down and simmer, partly covered, until tender all the way through, 1 to 1½ hours in all depending on the age of the beans. Add the salt in the last 15 minutes.
Cool them in their liquid in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours. Freeze them in their liquid in can-sized portions (about 1½ cups each).

stages.do: Boil hard, then simmer until tender

plan.thaw: Thaw in the refrigerator, or warm them straight from frozen in a covered pot.

keeps: Refrigerator: 3 to 4 days, as for other cooked leftovers (USDA).
Freezer: 3 to 4 months in their liquid (USDA’s time for leftovers).
recipes.scaling: 1 lb of dried beans makes about 6 cups cooked, about four 15-oz cans. Use a pot big enough that the beans stay covered by 2 inches of water.
safety: Never eat raw or undercooked dried beans. Soak at least 5 hours and boil in fresh water at least 30 minutes (FDA).
Cool in shallow containers and refrigerate within 2 hours (USDA).
recipes.yield: About 6 cups of cooked beans, drained: about the same as four 15-oz cans.
